ground_truth.title: Balanced Economy Project launches new report on how Big Finance blocks planet-friendly action
ground_truth.author: Scott Chipolina
ground_truth.main_content:
Hello and welcome back to The Counterbalance. We’re kicking off 2026 with a look at our new report: “Too Big To Cool The Planet: How Financial Power Blocks Planet-friendly Action and How to Break It"

This week, the Balanced Economy Project has published a new report titled “ Too Big To Cool The Planet, How Financial Power Blocks Planet-friendly Action and how to Break It ”, examining how the financial industry is a key driver of global warming. It is too big, is dominated by a few big, interconnected firms and shareholders, and has too much power.

The result is a self-reinforcing financial system that locks in extractive “growth”, high emissions and rising inequality. It is a system that is “too big to cool” the planet and serve society.

The report was presented this week at the Too Much Finance conference at the London School of Economics, alongside other research exploring how an outsized financial sector undermines economic performance, as well as how policy failures connected to the financial sector cause inequality and other social harms.

Finance is often talked about as a tool. A sector that can be steered or utilised by good or bad actors, but our new report shows why that framing needs revisiting.

Today, Big Finance has become one of the most powerful political and economic actors in its own right, shaping markets, influencing governments and determining the rules of the game. That power is now colliding head-on with the global effort to create a sustainable or “green” future.

It helps to grasp the scale of the system we are dealing with: by the end of 2024, global financial assets exceeded $500 trillion, while global GDP was valued at $110 trillion.

This did not happen by accident. From the late 1970s onwards, governments dismantled capital controls and liberalised financial markets, embracing an economic model that prioritised shareholder value and short-term profit rather than serving broader social goals. Over time, competition gave way to consolidation, and a small number of firms expanded across banking, asset management, insurance and private equity, absorbing rivals and integrating multiple financial functions under one roof.

One of the least visible, yet a defining feature of this system is ownership structures. Through common ownership the same small group of asset managers hold significant stakes in firms that are meant to compete in the same sector, while through universal ownership, those same firms hold positions across most of the economy. Together these enable financial actors to shape outcomes across markets and the wider economy, while remaining largely beyond the reach of existing regulatory frameworks.

Firms such as BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street — often referred to as the “Big Three” — are among the largest shareholders of major banks and financial institutions across the global economy. Collectively, these firms manage tens of trillions of dollars, and through their voting power at shareholder meetings they influence executive pay, merger activity, and long-term investment strategies.

In 2024 alone, BlackRock — via proxy advisers — voted on more than 150,000 shareholder proposals at nearly 17,000 shareholder meetings, engaging with almost 2,000 companies in 44 markets. This is not the invisible hand of the market at work, but a form of private governance exercised at a systemic level.

The financial sector is not a neutral intermediary in the climate transition. Our report shows that despite decades of warnings, global finance remains deeply entangled with fossil fuels precisely because the financial system is structurally oriented toward extraction rather than sustainability. Since the Paris Agreement came into effect in 2016, major banks have channelled $7.9 trillion into coal, oil, and gas. In 2024, the world’s largest banks still held $1.6 trillion in credit exposure tied to fossil fuel activities.

This is a reflection of where power and profitability lies in the modern financial system: the available returns from carbon-intensive activity dwarf the potential financial reward for renewable alternatives. Shareholder voting patterns among large US-based asset managers reflect a retreat from support for environmental resolutions in the boardroom, leaving fossil fuel finance largely intact.

Our report also shows how the influence of Big Finance is deployed politically when sustainability rules threaten to undermine profitability. We document how intense lobbying by financial and corporate interests has rolled back measures in the EU and US.

Measures designed to curb greenwashing have been diluted in the name of “competitiveness”, and in parallel, governments have increasingly turned to a de-risking strategy, shifting climate risks onto the public while sheltering the excessively powerful financial sector and enabling them to control the pace and direction of the climate action efforts.

The scale and reach of Big Finance gives a small number of financial actors the power to shape policy, regulation and capital flows at the same time. This systemic influence allows them to not just operate within markets, but to help construct and direct markets in a way that generates durable opportunities for wealth extraction. Financial power can shape new growth frontiers.

Nowhere are these dynamics more visible than in the rush to build out the artificial intelligence infrastructure– an industry that has quickly been framed as a strategic growth source for global finance even despite concerns about how extraordinarily energy and resource intensive these facilities are. Global electricity demand from data centres is projected to reach around 945 terawatt hours by 2030 — roughly equivalent to the total annual electricity consumption of Japan.

In the UK, data centre energy use rose by around 10 per cent in 2024, and electricity demand from the sector is expected to increase six-fold in the coming decade. Yet many of these developments in AI are being fast-tracked, with data centres designated as critical national infrastructure and granted priority access to power and land. And with scant regard to reinforcing dependence on global technology and finance monopolies.

In short, Big Finance has become too large, too interconnected, and too politically powerful to be treated as a neutral market any longer. Its dominance now acts as a seismic obstacle against meaningful environmental action, and that is why “Too Big to Cool the Planet” argues tackling global warming requires confronting financial power itself.

As governments around the world struggle to meet their climate commitments, the role of Big Finance — not just as a source of capital, but as a powerful political and economic actor in its own right — is becoming impossible to ignore. We highlight the central role of competition policy and enforcement, alongside financial regulation, in delivering a structural response to the systemic dominance of Big Finance.

In the weeks and months ahead, we will be publishing further material on how financial concentration, ownership structures and political capture are reshaping our climate pledges, undermining economic resilience and constraining democratic accountability. Understanding how financial power operates, and how it blocks meaningful climate action and societal goals, is essential if we are to achieve a truly sustainable and democratic economy.
